User authorization and preferences persist across turns. Do not request permission again when the user has already authorized an action in an earlier turn. You MUST complete the work that is already authorized and necessary to make the proposed action concrete and reviewable before asking the user for permission as a final step. tools.name: wait
tools.description:
Waits on a yielded `exec` cell and returns new output or completion.
- Use `wait` only after `exec` returns `Script running with cell ID ...`.
- `cell_id` identifies the running `exec` cell to resume.
- `yield_time_ms` controls how long to wait for more output before yielding again. Defaults to 10000 ms.
- `max_tokens` limits how much new output this wait call returns. Defaults to 10000 tokens.
- `terminate: true` stops the running cell; false or omitted waits for output.
- `wait` returns only the new output since the last yield, or the final completion or termination result for that cell.
- If the cell is still running, `wait` may yield again with the same `cell_id`.
- If the cell has already finished, `wait` returns the completed result and closes the cell.

cell_id.description: Identifier of the running exec cell.

max_tokens.description: Output token budget for this wait call. Defaults to 10000 tokens.

terminate.description: True stops the running exec cell; false or omitted waits for output.

yield_time_ms.description: Wait before yielding more output. Defaults to 10000 ms.

tools.description: Request user input for one to three short questions and wait for the response. This tool is only available in Plan mode.

questions.description: Questions to show the user. Prefer 1 and do not exceed 3

options.description: Provide 2-3 mutually exclusive choices. Put the recommended option first and suffix its label with "(Recommended)". Do not include an "Other" option in this list; the client will add a free-form "Other" option automatically.

description.description: One short sentence explaining impact/tradeoff if selected.

question.description: Single-sentence prompt shown to the user.

tools.description: Ask the user one or more questions during ongoing work. Use this tool only to request missing information, preferences, constraints, clarification, or approval. questions.description: One or more self-contained questions to present together, in display order.

options.description: Suggested answers, in display order. Put the recommended answer first; the first option is preselected by default. The user can select one option or enter a free-text answer. title.description: The complete question shown to the user, including any context needed to answer it.

duration_ms.description: How long to sleep in milliseconds. Must be between 1 and 43200000.

message.description: Message text to send to the target agent.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to send a follow-up task to (from spawn_agent).

tools.description: Interrupt an agent's current turn, if any, and return its previous status. The agent remains available for messages and follow-up tasks.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to interrupt (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: list_agents
tools.description: List live agents in the current root thread tree. Optionally filter by task-path prefix.

path_prefix.description: Task-path prefix filter without a trailing slash. Omit to list all live agents.

tools.description: Send a message to an existing agent. The message will be delivered promptly. Does not trigger a new turn.

message.description: Message text to queue on the target agent.

target.description: Relative or canonical task name to message (from spawn_agent).

fork_turns.description: Parent history to inherit. Defaults to `all`; use `none` to start without parent history. Only `all` and `none` are supported.

message.description: Initial plain-text task for the new agent.

model.description: Model override for the new agent. Omit unless an explicit override is needed.

reasoning_effort.description: Reasoning effort override for the new agent. Omit to inherit the parent effort.

task_name.description: Task name for the new agent. Use lowercase letters, digits, and underscores.

tools.name: wait_agent
tools.description: Wait for a mailbox update from any live agent, including queued messages and final-status notifications. timeout_ms.description: Timeout in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000, min 10000, max 3600000.

{"id": "codex-51152", "titulo": "app-server rejects every turn with "invalid cwd" once the daemon's own working directory is deleted, even when the request cwd is absolute", "texto": "## What happens

The shared app-server daemon starts with the working directory of the first `codex` invocation that spawns it. If that directory is later deleted (a removed git worktree, for example), every new `turn/start` on that daemon fails:

```
turn/start failed: invalid cwd: No such file or directory (os error 2) (code -32600)
```

This happens even though the turn's own `cwd` is an absolute path to a directory that exists. Every TUI attached to the daemon is affected until the daemon restarts. `codex resume <thread> --no-daemon` works around it for one session.

## Why

`resolve_request_cwd` (codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors.rs:629, rust-v0.160.0) resolves the request cwd with `AbsolutePathBuf::relative_to_current_dir`:

```rust
fn resolve_request_cwd(cwd: Option<PathBuf>) -> Result<Option<AbsolutePathBuf>, JSONRPCErrorError> {
    cwd.map(|cwd| {
        AbsolutePathBuf::relative_to_current_dir(path_utils::normalize_for_native_workdir(cwd))
            .map_err(|err| invalid_request(format!("invalid cwd: {err}")))
    })
    .transpose()
}
```

`relative_to_current_dir` (codex-rs/utils/absolute-path/src/lib.rs:87) calls `std::env::current_dir()?` unconditionally, before it looks at whether `path` is already absolute:

```rust
pub fn relative_to_current_dir<P: AsRef<Path>>(path: P) -> std::io::Result<Self> {
    Ok(Self::resolve_path_against_base(
        path,
        std::env::current_dir()?,
    ))
}
```

On Linux, `getcwd` fails with ENOENT when the process's cwd has been unlinked. So an absolute request path is rejected because of the daemon's own cwd, which the path does not depend on. The same call is used for `turn/start` (turn_processor.rs:621, :928) and thread resume (thread_processor.rs:3877).

## Reproduce

1. With no daemon running (`codex app-server daemon stop`), run `mkdir /tmp/x && cd /tmp/x && codex`. This starts the daemon with cwd `/tmp/x`. Exit the TUI.
2. `rm -rf /tmp/x`
3. `cd ~/some/repo && codex`, then send any prompt. The turn fails with `invalid cwd`.

## Expected

An absolute request cwd resolves without consulting the process cwd. Only a relative request cwd needs `current_dir()`, and its error could say that the daemon's working directory no longer exists.

Possible fix: in `relative_to_current_dir`, return `from_absolute_path(path)` when `path.is_absolute()`, and call `current_dir()` only for relative input.

## Related

The managed daemon and its updater both inherit the spawning terminal's cwd (`codex app-server daemon start`, and `Daemon::stop` leaves `daemon-updater.pid` running). So after `stop` + `start`, the next update recreates the daemon in the deleted directory again; only `daemon bootstrap` replaces both processes. Starting the managed daemon from a stable directory (for example `$CODEX_HOME`) regardless of the caller's cwd would remove the whole class.

Environment: codex-cli 0.160.0 (npm, linux-x64 musl), Ubuntu, managed app-server daemon (`codex app-server --listen unix:// --managed-daemon`).

Related report: #41559 (a session whose own cwd was removed). This issue is a different trigger: the request cwd exists and is absolute, and only the daemon process's cwd is gone.
"}
{"id": "codex-51153", "titulo": "Daemon bootstrap reports success while its updater exits with SUN_LEN under a deep CODEX_HOME (Linux)", "texto": "## Behaviour

On Linux with codex-cli 0.160.0, `app-server daemon bootstrap` successfully starts the managed app-server and records a daemon-updater PID, but the updater immediately exits when its Unix socket path exceeds the platform address limit. Its stderr contains `Error: path must be shorter than SUN_LEN`, and `daemon-updater.sock` never appears. The serving daemon survives, so an immediate PID-file check can incorrectly suggest that auto-update is working.

Observed in a private HOME under a pytest directory on 2026-10-03. No production daemon was stopped or restarted. The fixture's updater socket was longer than Linux's 108-byte Unix-address field. A short private HOME under disk TMPDIR produces a 99-byte updater address and is the proposed fixture workaround.

## Source

The updater binds its manual-update listener directly to `manual_update_socket_path()` in [update_loop.rs:118–128](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.0/codex-rs/app-server-daemon/src/update_loop.rs#L118).

That path is the updater PID-file path with a `.sock` extension, with no short-address mapping, in [lib.rs:993–995](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.160.0/codex-rs/app-server-daemon/src/lib.rs#L993).

The existing [deep control-socket path report](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/27765) describes daemon-client control addresses in 0.137/0.139 on macOS. This reproduction concerns the updater's separate socket in 0.160.0 on Linux; the app-server control socket itself works through its existing long-path fallback.

## Reproduction

1. Create a private HOME on disk with a long absolute path. Set `CODEX_HOME` to its `.codex` directory. Choose the length so `$CODEX_HOME/app-server-daemon/daemon-updater.sock` exceeds 108 bytes.
2. Copy the installed 0.160.0 app-server release into that private home's `packages/app-server-daemon/releases/0.160.0-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`, create `current` pointing at that release, and write that release name without a newline to `auto-update-version`. Never share writable package files or lifecycle state with the real HOME.
3. In the private `app-server-daemon/settings.json`, enable automatic updates and set shutdown grace to zero. Use a private config and no credentials.
4. Run the private binary with HOME, CODEX_HOME and TMPDIR explicitly set to private paths:

   ```sh
   "$private_codex" app-server daemon bootstrap
   ```

5. After bootstrap succeeds, read `app-server-daemon/daemon-updater.pid`, inspect that process, the updater socket, and `daemon-updater.stderr.log`.

Observed: the updater exits, the socket is absent, and stderr reports SUN_LEN; the daemon accepts a turn. Shortening only the private HOME makes the updater address fit. Stop only the private daemon and updater when finished.

## Expected

The updater should use a private short-address mapping for long paths, consistently with app-server control sockets. Bootstrap should not report a working updater merely because its PID record was published before startup failed. A regression should verify the updater stays alive and serves its socket after bootstrap with a long CODEX_HOME.

Environment: codex-cli 0.160.0 (npm, linux-x64 musl), Ubuntu, managed app-server daemon.
"}

{"id": "codex-51201", "titulo": "Managed daemon auto-update restart kills in-flight turns without a terminal event and reloads threads with default permissions instead of Full access (0.160.0 → 0.160.1, macOS)", "texto": "### What happened

macOS (arm64), managed app-server daemon with its own `CODEX_HOME`, several long-running desktop-app threads set to **Full access** (`permission_profile` type `disabled`, approval `never`).

1. The daemon's update loop installed **0.160.1** over **0.160.0**, and a minute later restarted the app-server.
2. Four threads had turns in progress. Each of those turns simply stops in its rollout: no `task_complete`, no `turn_aborted`, no error event. Nothing tells the thread (or the user) the turn was killed.
3. The restarted app-server emitted `thread_settings_applied` for each thread with `permission_profile` type `managed` and a `restricted` filesystem (workspace and tmp writable, no network), instead of the `disabled` profile the threads had before the restart.
4. The next turn on such a thread (started with `codex queue --thread …`) ran under that sandbox: no network, `.git` not writable. The agent could not reach anything outside the machine, including to ask for help. Nothing in the thread showed that its permissions had changed.

### Expected

- A daemon update does not restart the app-server under running turns (drain or hand off first), or at minimum records a terminal event with a reason on each interrupted turn.
- A thread's permission settings survive an app-server restart; a reloaded thread keeps the permissions it had.

### Workaround

Over the daemon's control socket, `turn/start` with `sandboxPolicy: {type: "dangerFullAccess"}` and `approvalPolicy: "never"` restores the previous behavior for that turn and subsequent turns.

### Versions

codex-cli 0.160.1, app-server 0.160.1 (updated from 0.160.0 by the managed daemon), macOS 26.6.2 arm64.

### Related

#45665 (turn lost when the app-server is replaced), #51098 (`--yolo` ignored on the managed daemon), #48195 (self-updating daemon as the default).
"}

[Official hook documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/hooks) describes supported explicit denial, callback failures that can leave actions unblocked, incomplete tool-path coverage, and exceptions to the ordinary hook path. [Plugin documentation](https://developers.openai.com/plugins/build/plugins) also requires separate trust for plugin hooks. ## Smallest host-owned repair requested

1. Add an explicit required-policy admission contract, separate from ordinary advisory hooks. This is a proposed capability, not an existing setting.
2. Bind admission to the actual thread, turn, original outcome, exact operation/payload, authority revision and single-use request identity.
3. Enforce it at every relevant native dispatch path, including nested code-mode calls. Unsupported paths must be exposed and denied when required by policy, rather than silently bypassing admission.
4. Deny on missing/untrusted/modified authority, missing checker, launcher failure, checker crash, invalid response, deadline expiry or lost policy transport.
5. Apply the corresponding original-outcome gate before final bytes are rendered. Uncertain continuation effects must remain reserved across restart and require authoritative reconciliation.
6. Expose authenticated invocation/decision observations and a supported way to bind the current conversation. Caller-created environment secrets, local brands and authored JSON must not qualify as production host evidence.

Existing repository adapters already exercise sealed role/skill bodies, exact byte binding, issued guards, durable duplicate suppression and uncertain-effect reconciliation. They can be integration targets, but cannot establish their own mandatory invocation.

## Acceptance tests

- A positive exact-bound admission executes one harmless action once.
- Explicit denial and every unavailable/error path execute zero actions.
- Wrong-thread, wrong-turn, changed payload, changed authority, replay and expired admission are denied.
- Nested/local/MCP/subagent paths cannot bypass the required boundary; unsupported hosted paths are explicitly identified.
- An unfinished original outcome cannot release final bytes; continuation is acknowledged and duplicate-safe.
- Restart preserves reservations and original-parent identity.
- Tests inspect native dispatch and rendered-output evidence, not simulated assistant prose alone.

## Safety and disclosure

Persistent configuration, execution policy, signing-service/trust-authority work and native Stop enablement were excluded. Hashes of the three named configuration files match before/after the fresh probe; this is not a whole-host mutation audit. No production guard was installed. Private prompts, account information, credentials and conversation identifiers are intentionally excluded from this report.

Source review found that a project-wide alignment command selected one assistant identity using only the repository working directory. Other role-specific conversations can share that directory. Prompt text, titles, transcript text, environment flags and caller-authored role fields cannot supply that identity.

{"id": "codex-55834", "titulo": "[Bug] Non-atomic write of ~/.codex/config.toml leads to 0x00 null-byte corruption and unrecoverable startup crash on sudden power loss", "texto": "### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1016.6573.0 (Codex CLI v0.150.1)

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Plus

### What platform is your computer?

 Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26300.0 x64

### What issue are you seeing?

When the host computer experiences a sudden unexpected power loss or hard shutdown while Codex is running or updating, the configuration file `~/.
  codex/config.toml` gets corrupted with null bytes (`0x00`).

    Upon subsequent launches of either the Codex CLI or ChatGPT Desktop, the TOML lexer/parser fails immediately with a fatal syntax error:

    ```text
    › Error loading config.toml:
    C:\Users\<username>\.codex\config.toml:1:4537: key with no value, expected `=`

  Both the desktop application and CLI enter an unrecoverable crash loop. Neither application provides a safe-mode fallback, automatic configuration
  repair, or backup quarantine, leaving users completely locked out until they manually inspect and reset the corrupted file.



### What steps can reproduce the bug?

```markdown
    The crash can be reliably reproduced by simulating an interrupted/unflushed file write with null bytes:

    1. Open PowerShell and write null bytes into `config.toml`:
    ```powershell
    [System.IO.File]::WriteAllBytes("$HOME\.codex\config.toml", [byte[]](0..4535 | ForEach-Object { 0 }))

  2. Attempt to launch Codex CLI or Codex Doctor:

    codex doctor

  Or launch the ChatGPT / Codex Desktop app.

  3. Result: The process crashes immediately at startup with C:\Users\<username>\.codex\config.toml:1:4537: key with no value, expected =.



### What is the expected behavior?

 ```markdown
    1. **Atomic Configuration Writes**: Configuration updates should never write directly in-place without syncing. Best practice is to write to a
  temporary file (`config.toml.tmp`), flush buffers (`FlushFileBuffers` / `fsync`), and perform an atomic replacement (`ReplaceFile` / `MoveFileEx`). This
  guarantees that an abrupt power cut or termination leaves the previous intact version intact.
    2. **Graceful Corruption Recovery**: If `config.toml` cannot be parsed (e.g. contains binary null bytes or invalid TOML), Codex should:
       - Catch the error gracefully instead of terminating the host process.
       - Quarantine the corrupted file (e.g. rename to `config.toml.corrupted.<timestamp>`).
       - Fall back to clean default in-memory configuration.
       - Prompt the user with a notification offering to reset or repair the configuration.


### Additional information


    Forensic analysis from Windows Event Logs on the affected machine confirmed:
    - **Event ID 6008**: Unexpected system shutdown recorded at `14:22:17`.
    - **Event ID 41 (Kernel-Power)**: `BugcheckCode: 0`, confirming a hardware power drop / battery cutoff without any OS crash or Blue Screen (no
  minidump was generated).
    - At that exact moment, the Windows Store package `9PLM9XGG6VKS-OpenAI.Codex` had just completed installing (`14:21:46`) and background provisioning
  was active.
    - On Windows NTFS, an ungraceful power loss between cluster allocation and buffer flush causes the file metadata to retain the allocated size (4,536
  bytes) while disk contents remain zeroed out. The TOML parser then treats all 4,536 null bytes as an unterminated bare key name, reaching EOF at column

{"id": "codex-51098", "titulo": "0.160.0: --yolo ignored for new threads when TUI runs on managed app-server daemon / --remote", "texto": "### What version of Codex is running?

codex-cli 0.160.0 (Homebrew cask), managed app-server daemon 0.160.0, macOS 27.0 (arm64)

### What issue are you seeing?

On 0.160.0, `codex --yolo` no longer gives **new** threads full access when the TUI runs on the managed app-server daemon. The thread is created with `approval_mode = on-request` and `sandbox_policy = {"type":"managed", file_system: restricted (cwd writable), "network":"restricted"}`. Commands that need network or local sockets fail (e.g. a local device bridge on `127.0.0.1:8710` → `Connect server failed`).

This is related to #49865 / #49088 (permissions lost after a daemon restart), but here the thread is **new**, not resumed:

1. `codex --yolo` started at 12:37:18. The thread was created at 12:37:19 **inside the long-running managed daemon process** (logs_2.sqlite shows it under the daemon's pid, not the TUI's), and `state_5.sqlite` records `approval_mode=on-request`, `sandbox_policy.type=managed`, `network=restricted`.
2. The same happens through a wrapper that starts its own app-server with `codex app-server -c approval_policy="never" -c sandbox_mode="danger-full-access" --listen unix://…` and then attaches `codex --remote unix://…`. The TUI (`client_name="codex-tui"`) creates the thread itself, and the thread ends up with `approval_mode=never` but `sandbox_policy` managed/restricted — the server-side `-c sandbox_mode="danger-full-access"` is not applied. Every `TurnInput` has `sandbox_policy: None, permission_profile: None`, so the restricted policy from thread creation sticks.
3. Additionally (= #49088/#49865): an older thread that had been running as `DangerFullAccess` on the daemon dropped to `WorkspaceWrite` after `codex app-server daemon restart`.

`~/.codex/config.toml` has no `sandbox_mode` / `approval_policy`. Before upgrading to 0.160.0 (from 0.159.2), `--yolo` in both setups gave full access.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. No `sandbox_mode`/`approval_policy` in `~/.codex/config.toml`; managed daemon running.
2. `codex --yolo`, start a new chat, ask it to run `curl -sI https://example.com` (or connect to any local TCP port).
3. Observe approval prompts / network denied; `select approval_mode, sandbox_policy from threads order by created_at desc limit 1` in `~/.codex/state_5.sqlite` shows on-request + managed/restricted.

### What is the expected behavior?

`--yolo` (and `-c sandbox_mode="danger-full-access"` on the app-server) should result in `approval_mode=never` + `danger-full-access` for threads created from that TUI, regardless of whether the TUI runs in-process, on the managed daemon, or via `--remote`.

### Additional information

Workaround: put `sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"` and `approval_policy = "never"` in `~/.codex/config.toml` and restart the daemon.
"}

The source permits one traversal: five opens (`/`, `Users`, the account component, `Library`, `Mobile Documents`); root `O_RDONLY | O_DIRECTORY`; later opens add `O_NOFOLLOW` and use the preceding directory descriptor. At most two traversal descriptors coexist, with at most five close attempts. There is one invocation, no explicit retries, children, threads, watchdog or installed timer. {"id": "codex-51144", "titulo": "[macOS app] Readable local chat rejects submissions with thread_not_found; archive/unarchive restores loaded state", "texto": "### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Desktop release `26.930.31730` (build `12947`), verified from the installed application metadata and corroborated by the desktop session log. The About dialog was not inspected. The affected thread's stored runtime version is `0.159.0-alpha.12.1`; this is session metadata, not a fresh executable-version check.

### What subscription do you have?

Not collected for this report.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS `27.0.1`, Apple Silicon. Requested `uname -mprs` output: `Darwin 27.0.0 arm64 arm`. Affected chat host: `local`; stored history mode: `paginated`.

### What issue are you seeing?

An existing local chat remained listed in the sidebar and its recent history was readable, but submitting a new message repeatedly failed:

```text
thread not found: <affected-thread>
```

Desktop logs show JSON-RPC `-32600` with `failureReason=thread_not_found` on `turn/start` and `mcpServerStatus/list`, while `thread/read` and history pagination calls for the same thread succeeded.

The saved thread was not archived. Its rollout file existed and was readable (approximately 22 MB), and the thread API reported `notLoaded`. Simply navigating to the chat again did not change the reported `notLoaded` state. Archive → unarchive → reopen subsequently triggered a successful `thread/resume`, and independent status checks reported `idle`.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

**Reproduction status:** the submission failure repeated in one affected existing chat. A reliable way to put a fresh chat into the same broken state has not been established. The steps below reproduce the failure only when that state is already present.

**Preconditions:** a persistent local chat with completed turns, readable history, `archived=false`, and runtime status `notLoaded`, while the desktop still allows submission. No original prompt or private transcript is required to describe the failure.

1. Select an existing local chat that has completed previous turns.
2. Attempt to submit a new message. For a maintainer retest, use a neutral diagnostic input such as `Reply with OK.`; that prompt was not used in this incident, and prompt independence has not been experimentally verified.
3. Observe `thread not found: <affected-thread>`.
4. Retry submission: the same error recurs.
5. Read the chat through the thread-reading interface: recent completed turns are still accessible.
6. Reopen the chat through navigation: it remains `notLoaded`.
7. Archive the affected unloaded chat, unarchive it, and reopen it.
8. Observe a successful `thread/resume` and status `idle`.

**Observed lifecycle clue:** the same chat had a successful `thread/resume` earlier, followed by a successful `thread/unsubscribe` approximately seven minutes before the failed submissions. No intervening `thread/resume` response for this chat was recorded. Two `No promise for request ID` errors appeared immediately after the unsubscribe responses; their request IDs were not correlated, so they are a clue rather than an established cause. The action that initiated unsubscribe and whether it caused the loss of runtime state remain unknown.

**Maintainer regression-test proposal (not executed):** use a synthetic saved chat in an isolated fixture; remove its loaded runtime session through a test hook while keeping its history and the desktop's displayed chat/composer state. Attempt submission through the desktop. Assert that the client resumes the chat and waits for success before `turn/start`, rather than surfacing `thread_not_found`. This isolates the suspected stale-state boundary; merely calling `turn/start` against an unloaded fixture is not by itself proof of a desktop bug.

For an already initialized app-server test connection, the relevant request shapes are:

```jsonl
{"id":1,"method":"thread/read","params":{"threadId":"<synthetic-saved-thread-id>","includeTurns":false}}
{"id":2,"method":"turn/start","params":{"threadId":"<synthetic-saved-thread-id>","input":[{"type":"text","text":"Reply with OK.","text_elements":[]}]}}
```

Send these sequentially and await each response. The placeholder must refer to a real synthetic fixture, not a randomly invented ID. These shapes were checked against the public protocol schema; this is a diagnostic sketch, not a tested end-to-end reproducer. Use a stubbed model in the fixture so a successful submission does not start real model work.

### What is the expected behavior?

A saved, readable, unarchived chat should be resumed before the client sends operations that require a loaded session. If the runtime session has disappeared, the client should reconcile its cached state and offer recovery or resume the existing chat safely. Users should not need an archive/unarchive cycle to restore an existing conversation.

### Additional information

Sanitized diagnostic timeline from the same desktop session. Absolute timestamps are omitted; elapsed times are rounded relative to the affected chat's successful unsubscribe. Every row refers to the same chat, aliased `<affected-thread>`.

| Approximate elapsed time | Operation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | `thread/unsubscribe` | Success |
| +6m 35s | `turn/start` | `-32600`, `thread_not_found` |
| +6m 42s | `mcpServerStatus/list` | `-32600`, `thread_not_found` |
| +6m 42s | `turn/start` | `-32600`, `thread_not_found` |
| +7m 08s | `thread/read` | Success |
| +7m 08s | `thread/turns/list` | Success |
| +8m 22s | `thread/archive` | Success |
| +8m 23s | `thread/unarchive` | Success |
| +8m 24s | `thread/resume` | Success |

**Recovery verification:** archive/unarchive was performed through the desktop's supported thread-management tools. After reopening, both `wait_threads` and `list_threads` reported `idle`; the latest completed turn remained readable. No new prompt was sent merely to test recovery, so a subsequent successful `turn/start` was not independently verified. No databases or transcript contents were manually edited.

**Possible cause, unconfirmed:** disagreement between the client's cached chat state and the app-server's loaded-session state. The evidence establishes the read/start mismatch and successful reload, not the cause of the original unload.

**Related reports and duplicate search:** searched the issue tracker for `thread not found` together with `archive`, `unarchive`, and `unsubscribe`. #30710 describes a Windows stored-chat submission/resume race; #42604 describes macOS Goal/multi-agent history desynchronization; #45213 describes a…2028 tokens truncated… cluster allocation and buffer flush causes the file metadata to retain the allocated size (4,536
  bytes) while disk contents remain zeroed out. The TOML parser then treats all 4,536 null bytes as an unterminated bare key name, reaching EOF at column
  4537 and throwing `key with no value, expected =`.
"}

{"id": "codex-56393", "titulo": "CLI: attach a second terminal to a running session without closing the first (at least read-only)", "texto": "### What variant of Codex are you using?

Codex CLI / terminal TUI.

### What feature would you like to see?

Please add a supported way to open the same currently running Codex session in a second terminal while leaving the first terminal open and usable.

Read-only observation would be the minimum useful feature. If safe shared interaction is supported, being able to send messages from the second terminal would be welcome too.

### Desired workflow

1. Start an interactive Codex session in terminal A and let it work.
2. Open terminal B and select or specify that same active session.
3. See its existing conversation and follow new messages and tool activity live, with independent scrolling.
4. Keep terminal A connected and the ongoing work uninterrupted.
5. Close terminal B without stopping the session or disconnecting terminal A.

The second view should attach to the same live session, without creating a fork, starting a separate agent run, or requiring the first terminal to exit or release ownership.

### Possible interface

For example, `codex attach <session-id> --read-only` or a read-only attachment option in the session picker. These are suggested interfaces, not existing commands.

Optional writable attachment could allow input from either terminal, with consistent shared history and clear handling of concurrent messages and approvals. Read-only attachment alone would already solve the core need.

### Why this matters

I want to consult and follow an ongoing session from another terminal without leaving the original one. This is a request for a built-in session viewer/attachment workflow, rather than having to inspect raw session files or arrange terminal multiplexing in advance.

### Related requests

- #32445 requests terminal TUI attachment to an existing Remote Control chat.
- #52015 requests a read-only Android view of an active VS Code chat.
- #15896 requests a parallel agent session for interrogating/monitoring a working agent.

This request focuses on attaching a second terminal directly to the same live CLI session, with read-only access as the minimum and shared input as an optional extension."}
